content: Acute sinusitis is a frequent condition that leads to numerous visits to primary care providers. It often causes significant discomfort and can result in individuals missing work or school. Researchers aimed to determine whether intranasal corticosteroids (INCS) are effective in alleviating the symptoms of acute sinusitis in both adults and children. To investigate this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering studies published up to May 2013. The review focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared the use of INCS to either a placebo or no treatment in individuals diagnosed with acute sinusitis. The diagnosis of acute sinusitis was confirmed through clinical evaluation and supported by radiological evidence or nasal endoscopy. The primary outcome of interest was the proportion of participants who experienced either complete resolution or improvement of their symptoms. Secondary outcomes included adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation, participant drop-out rates, relapse rates, complications, and the time taken to return to work or school. Four RCTs, involving a total of 1,943 participants with acute sinusitis, met the inclusion criteria for this review. These studies were well-designed, double-blind trials that compared INCS to placebo or no intervention over treatment durations of 15 or 21 days. The rates of participants lost to follow-up varied across the studies, ranging from 7% to 41%. When the results of three trials were combined in a meta-analysis, it was found that participants treated with INCS were more likely to experience symptom resolution or improvement compared to those receiving placebo (73% versus 66.4%; risk ratio [RR] 1.11; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.04 to 1.18). Higher doses of INCS appeared to have a greater effect on symptom improvement or complete relief. For example, mometasone furoate at a dose of 400 µg showed a stronger benefit (RR 1.10; 95% CI 1.02 to 1.18) compared to a dose of 200 µg (RR 1.04; 95% CI 0.98 to 1.11). No significant adverse events were reported in the studies, and there were no notable differences in drop-out rates, recurrence rates, or complications between the treatment groups. Similarly, no significant differences were observed between groups receiving higher versus lower doses of INCS. The authors concluded that while the current evidence is limited to cases of acute sinusitis confirmed by radiological or endoscopic methods, it supports the use of INCS either as a standalone treatment or as an adjunct to antibiotics. Clinicians should consider the modest but clinically meaningful benefits of INCS while also weighing the potential for minor adverse effects when deciding on treatment options.
